topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Fractions
topic.scope: meaning of fraction, equivalent fractions, like and unlike, comparing, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions

misconceptions.statement: Any division of a shape into the required number of parts represents a fraction, even if parts are unequal.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the count of parts rather than the area or size of each part.
misconceptions.fix: A fraction represents a part of a whole only when the whole is divided into equal-sized parts.

probe.question: If a circle is cut into two unequal pieces, is one piece 1/2?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because there are two pieces.

misconceptions.root_belief: quantity is just a count of items

misconceptions.statement: The denominator is the total number of parts across all wholes shown in a diagram.
misconceptions.why: Students count every individual piece they see instead of identifying what constitutes one single 'whole'.
misconceptions.fix: The denominator tells us how many equal parts ONE whole is divided into.

probe.question: If two pizzas are each cut into 4 slices, and I have 5 slices, what is the denominator?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A fraction is two separate whole numbers sitting on top of each other.
misconceptions.why: The notation uses two whole numbers, leading students to treat them as independent entities.
misconceptions.fix: A fraction is a single number representing a single point on a number line.

probe.question: Is 3/4 one number or two numbers?

misconceptions.statement: 1/5 is greater than 1/4 because 5 is greater than 4.
misconceptions.why: Students apply whole number magnitude rules to the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: When the numerator is the same, a larger denominator means the whole is divided into more (and thus smaller) pieces.

misconceptions.statement: Adding the same number to the numerator and denominator creates an equivalent fraction.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the idea of 'doing the same thing to top and bottom' from multiplication to addition.
misconceptions.fix: Equivalent fractions are only formed by multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.

misconceptions.statement: To add fractions, you add the numerators and add the denominators.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the numerator and denominator as independent whole numbers to be added separately.
misconceptions.fix: When adding like fractions, add only the numerators and keep the common denominator the same.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Multiplying a number by a fraction always results in a larger product.
misconceptions.why: In whole numbers, multiplication (repeated addition) always increases the value.
misconceptions.fix: Multiplying by a proper fraction (less than 1) results in a product smaller than the original number.

misconceptions.statement: Dividing a number by a fraction always results in a smaller quotient.
misconceptions.why: In whole numbers, division (sharing) always results in a smaller value.
misconceptions.fix: Dividing by a proper fraction (less than 1) results in a quotient larger than the original number.

misconceptions.statement: A mixed number like 2 1/3 means 2 multiplied by 1/3.
misconceptions.why: In algebra, placing terms side-by-side implies multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: A mixed number is the sum of a whole number and a proper fraction.

misconceptions.statement: The reciprocal of a whole number like 4 is just 4.
misconceptions.why: Students don't realize whole numbers can be written as fractions with a denominator of 1.
misconceptions.fix: The reciprocal of a whole number 'n' is 1/n, because n can be written as n/1.

misconceptions.statement: Fractions can only be added if their numerators are the same.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between the roles of numerators and denominators in the addition algorithm.
misconceptions.fix: Fractions must have the same denominator (be 'like' fractions) to be added directly.

probe.question: Can you add 1/3 and 1/4 directly because they both have 1 on top?

misconceptions.statement: A fraction with 'larger' numbers is always bigger than one with 'smaller' numbers (e.g., 10/20 > 1/2).
misconceptions.why: Focusing on the absolute magnitude of the digits rather than the ratio.
misconceptions.fix: The value of a fraction depends on the ratio of the numerator to the denominator, not the size of the digits.
